It appears that nearly all members of this family form
arbuscular mycorrhizae: the hyphae interact with the root cells forming a mutually beneficial
association in which the plants supply the carbon source and energy in the form of carbohydrates to
the fungus, and the fungus supplies essential minerals from the soil to the plant. The exception is
Geosiphon pyriformis, which hosts the cyanobacterium Nostoc as an endosymbiont. The glomeromycetes do not reproduce sexually and do not survive without the presence of plant roots. Although they have coenocytic hyphae like the zygomycetes, they do not form zygospores.

Stage 3: Regeneration
Interestingly, at this point, only one of the G3P molecules leaves the Calvin cycle and is sent to the
cytoplasm to contribute to the formation of other compounds needed by the plant. Because the G3P
exported from the chloroplast has three carbon atoms, it takes three “turns” of the Calvin cycle to fix
enough net carbon to export one G3P. But each turn makes two G3Ps, thus three turns make six G3Ps. One is exported while the remaining five G3P molecules remain in the cycle and are used to regenerate
RuBP, which enables the system to prepare for more CO  to be fixed. Three more molecules of ATP are
used in these regeneration reactions.

evidence.evidence: It appears that nearly all members of this family form arbuscular mycorrhizae: the hyphae interact with the root cells forming a mutually beneficial association in which the plants supply the carbon source and energy in the form of carbohydrates to the fungus, and the fungus supplies essential minerals from the soil to the plant.
In exchange, the plant supplies the products of photosynthesis to fuel the metabolism of the fungus.
The Calvin cycle, which takes place in the stroma, uses energy derived from these compounds to make G3P from CO2.
In the case of photosynthesis, light energy is converted into chemical energy, which photoautotrophs use to build basic carbohydrate molecules (Figure 8.9).

In the stroma, in addition to CO2, two other components are present to initiate the light-independent reactions: an enzyme called ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO), and three molecules of ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP).

Sexual reproduction starts with the development of special hyphae from either one of two types of mating strains (Figure 24.14).

The spores in each ascus contain the meiotic products of a single diploid nucleus. The ascospores are then released, germinate, and form hyphae that are disseminated in the environment and start new mycelia (Figure 24.15).
The Phylum Ascomycota, which is characterized by the formation of an ascus (plural, asci), a sac-like structure that contains haploid ascospores.
Thousands of asci fill a fruiting body called the ascocarp.
